apparatus: 45 known-answer/runtime controls and seven frozen consumers verified

mechanisms.finding: Does inferring a source explain uptake better than one fixed trust? In this constructed mechanism, source inference improves native property log loss by 0.102, 0.115 and 0.249 nats against trusts 0.2, 0.54 and 0.9. Steering detection rises from 13.4% without records to 100% with 32 records. The proposed competence ordering of discrepancy-curve peaks fails: with long records, competent informers peak earlier than weak informers on the tested grid. No universal trust crossover or broad architecture claim follows.

Do costly departures identify preferences more efficiently? Effort weighting narrows the constructed set-point intervals but lowers coverage relative to exact unit weighting. At 32 native records, coverage remains 98.26% and future-choice log loss improves by only 0.0090 nats. The direct reader already trails inside its training range and does not worsen after larger perturbations, so the proposed inside-parity/outside-failure account is not established. These are finite constructed-mechanism results.

Do shared processes and records help different inference targets? In the independent constructed world, eight preference records improve loss by 0.423 nats without a shared library and 0.460 with one. A reliable shared-library benefit itself is not established when similarity is hidden. Disclosing the sharing relation identifies the binary preference without records, and a coupled preference witness also helps. The unconditional claim that similarity cannot inform preferences fails; the result depends on what is disclosed and coupled.

Does recognizing steering reduce content uptake while preserving technique? With a correctly mapped signature, the constructed full-library reader changes its content belief by 0.0167 on average versus 0.1606 for the missing-process reader, while technique-production probability is 89.94% versus 89.46%. But the content gap persists without the signature, so the proposed vanishing-gap control fails. This supports a qualified library-and-signature mechanism, not a clean signature-only explanation.

Does withdrawal protect uptake at matched technique? In one fixed mixture comparison with goal-bearing procedures, withdrawal reduces purpose and value memory change by 0.120 and 0.112 while technique accuracy differs by only 0.60 percentage points. Purpose-recognition loss is not established in that comparison. The separate physical learner retains unwanted uptake when useful procedures carry it. These are constructed-mechanism results; they do not establish disgust or a universal protection-with-recognition-cost tradeoff.

Can acquisition route predict a choice after need satisfaction? The two-route reader beats both single-route assumptions on post-devaluation choice loss in every tested condition. Under broken contingency its loss is 0.456 nats, versus 0.926 for the model-based-only reader and 1.212 for association-only. Yet observational aliases keep route probability exactly at one half. This is a constructed-mechanism prediction result, not proof that the historical route is always identifiable.

Does joint inference improve recovery across a goal hierarchy? Joint reading improves internal-node probability forecasts over the one-direction ablations, but bottom-up inference already matches it at the root. Removing distant evidence can hurt more than removing immediate-child evidence, and root accuracy is not monotone in every coverage series. These are finite constructed-tree results: marginal node scores do not establish a joint-prediction advantage or mathematical smoothness.
